issues.legal_issue: A purchaser at a statutory auction acquires title upon confirmation of the sale when the full purchase price has been paid, even if the sale certificate is issued later.
material_facts: The property was sold by public auction, and the purchaser paid the full purchase price before the bid was approved.
The bid was approved on October 3, 1956, and the sale certificate was issued later, recording the date of confirmation.
The tenant was told to pay rent to the purchaser from the date of confirmation and treated the purchaser as landlord from that date.
issues.conclusion: Title passed to the purchaser on confirmation of the sale, so the purchaser could claim rent from that date and maintain the eviction proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rules 90 and 92 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, title under the statutory auction process passes when the full price has been paid and the sale is confirmed; issuance of the certificate thereafter is not essential to the transfer. The fiction in Section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which dates title from the auction, does not apply because the Rules contain no such provision. Bombay Salt and Chemical Industries v. L. J. Johnson did not decide when title passes where the price had been paid and the sale confirmed. The Court agreed generally with the observations in Roshanlal Goswami v. Gobind Ram and referred to Jaimal Singh v. Smt. Gini Devi.

predicates.statutory_auction_title_dispute: The dispute concerns when a purchaser acquired title through an official auction sale governed by a statutory sale process.
predicates.full_purchase_price_paid: The purchaser paid the full purchase price for the property.
predicates.sale_confirmed: The competent authority approved or confirmed the auction sale.

issues.definition: When a title dispute concerns a statutory auction sale, full payment and confirmation mean that title passes upon confirmation.

issues.legal_issue: A rent controller must order eviction when the tenant has defaulted in paying rent and has not made the full statutory cure at the first hearing.
material_facts: The rent was determined to be Rs. 12 per month, and the purchaser was entitled to rent from the date the sale was confirmed.

The tenant's second court deposit was made after the eviction application had been filed, and the Controller found the total amount deposited was short by Rs. 4-12-0 of the amount required, including rent, interest and application costs.
There was no proof of money-order tenders covering the relevant period.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to relief from forfeiture, and the eviction order was required to stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, provides for eviction for non-payment of rent, subject to the proviso deeming the tenant to have paid in time if, at the first hearing, the tenant pays or tenders the arrears, interest and application costs. In Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, this Court held that a rent controller must order eviction when the statutory default is established and the tenant has not made the required cure; the decision was binding. The Court treated that rule as precluding relief from forfeiture in this case.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and rent_default and not full_cure_at_first_hearing

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking to evict a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.rent_default: The tenant failed to pay or tender rent within the time allowed for payment.
predicates.full_cure_at_first_hearing: At the first hearing, the tenant paid or tendered all arrears, interest and application costs.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction proceeding, an uncured rent default requires eviction, while a full cure at the first hearing means the default is treated as timely payment.
